Contents

  1. Before You BeginWhat this book is about, how it is laid out, and the people and the company whose project runs through it.
1

The problem worth solving

Anaya notices something odd in the chat, and learns how a product person decides what to build, and what to leave alone.

  1. 1The Number in the ChatA product manager finds identity numbers in a week of customer chats. She must decide if this is worth a year of work. You learn what personal data is. You learn why you count before you decide, how to pick between problems, and how to write a decision down.11 min read✓ read
  2. 2Four Questions Before BuildingAn engineer tests a promising idea against the four ways a product can fail. His example is a feature that nobody found. You learn the three stages of making a product, the four product risks, and how selling to people differs from selling to companies.9 min read✓ read
  3. 3Asking About YesterdayA first talk with a colleague gets only agreement. Five better talks get proof. You learn how to ask people about their past, how to read what they were trying to get done, and how to find the one assumption to test first.10 min read✓ read
  4. 4Who Else Is Standing HereThe head of compliance says a "yes, but" to the tool. It sets one hard rule. Then Anaya checks if the tool already exists. She counts the market from the ground up. She studies the rivals, even the one that is not a product.10 min read✓ read
  5. 5Choosing What Not to DoA list of nine good ideas is not a strategy. A retired teacher asks one question, and it leads Anaya to write a real strategy. She picks one small first target and one number for success. She names the product. She ranks the work with scores, and she is ready to overrule them.8 min read✓ read
  6. 6A Plan Others Can BelieveA strategy is only a sentence until other people can act on it. Anaya learns to promise results, not dates. She writes goals as numbers that can be measured. She maps who can say no. She also runs a meeting that pretends the project has already failed.11 min read✓ read
  7. 7Writing It Down So Others Can Build ItAn engineer draws the guard on a napkin. The product manager turns the drawing into a recipe card that a stranger could cook from. You learn the four parts of the guard, how to say when work is done, how to build a thin first version, and what a paper test shows that a meeting cannot.11 min read✓ read
2

Meeting the machine

What a language model is, how to talk to it, and how to tell whether it did well.

  1. 8What the Machine IsA product manager has said "powered by AI" for two years. She tries to explain it and cannot. We build the answer from the ground up: language models, tokens, the context window, attention, how a model is made and used, and the two kinds of AI.9 min read✓ read
  2. 9The First ConversationAn engineer shows the product manager one request to a language model and the reply that comes back. The bill that comes with the reply teaches as much as the answer. You learn about APIs, JSON, how to read a few lines of Python, API keys, the usage block, and why a sure-sounding answer is not proof.8 min read✓ read
  3. 10A Mind With No MemoryA language model is like a goldfish. It forgets everything after each message. A chatbot only seems to remember, because the app sends the whole chat again each time. You see how that works, what it costs, and why it makes the privacy problem bigger.6 min read✓ read
  4. 11Giving InstructionsThe team asks a language model to do the guard's work for the first time. It fails in three different ways. You learn what a prompt is, and what a system prompt, temperature, hallucination and worked example are. You also see that an instruction makes a failure rarer. It does not take away the cause.8 min read✓ read
  5. 12Knowing Whether It WorksThe team stops trusting how an answer feels. They write down the right answers before they look at the tool's. You learn test sets, answer keys, scoreboards, changing one thing at a time, and the five kinds of job a request can be.8 min read✓ read
  6. 13Sorting and SummarisingOne job has a right answer and one does not. The team tests a sorter and finds a failure that one score was hiding. Then they check a summary for the facts it left out. You meet classifiers, the cost of each kind of error, and the must-keep list.7 min read✓ read
3

Finding things, and the whole machine

Long documents, search by words and by meaning, and how the parts join into one working system.

  1. 14Too Long to Read at OnceAnaya wants to know how the chatbot answers from Sahaj's own documents. She cuts a policy with scissors, three times. You learn why long documents are cut into pieces, what chunking is, and why no way of cutting is the right one.7 min read✓ read
  2. 15Finding by WordsAnaya plays the search box. She learns why the oldest way of finding text fails the customers who need help most. She also learns why it is exactly right for an identity number. You meet keyword search and its silent failure.6 min read✓ read
  3. 16Finding by MeaningA bazaar where shops of one trade share a lane gives Anaya the picture she needs. It shows the idea that rescued search, and a number to be wary of. You meet embeddings and similarity scores.7 min read✓ read
  4. 17How Good Is GoodA founder asks the question every AI project meets in the end. The answer turns out to be two numbers, a choice between them that is not an engineer's to make, and a figure Anaya had quoted without checking. You meet recall and precision.8 min read✓ read
  5. 18The Whole MachineAnaya has now built every part of the chatbot by hand. She draws the whole thing from memory, and it gets a name. You meet RAG, the quiet ways it goes wrong, and every place a customer's words get copied.7 min read✓ read
  6. 19Answers a Program Can UseA paragraph is fine for a person, but a program cannot read it. You see why asking nicely for JSON is not enough. A schema is like a form with fixed boxes, and it removes a whole family of errors. Even then the box can hold a wrong answer, so you design the form to leave no room to invent.8 min read✓ read
4

Giving it work to do

Tools, thinking models, hostile text, grading at scale, and what it all costs.

  1. 20Giving the Machine HandsA twelve-digit order number can look like an Aadhaar number. A check-digit rule clears most look-alikes. For the rest, the only way to be sure is to look the number up. You meet tool calling, tool descriptions, AI agents and step limits. You see how a loop's cost climbs, and the difference between actions that read and actions that do.8 min read✓ read
  2. 21Long Windows, Careful RoomsA vendor says a huge context window means you do not need retrieval. A product manager asks two questions that end the meeting. You see why what goes into a request matters more than how much fits. You meet context engineering, token budgets, caching and compaction.7 min read✓ read
  3. 22Machines That Think FirstSome models work out the answer on rough paper before they reply. They get the hard cases right, but they take eleven seconds. This chapter covers reasoning models, what thinking costs, latency, streaming, and a design where the costly careful judge never makes a customer wait.7 min read✓ read
  4. 23Searching BetterA customer is told last year's late fee. Four ways to improve search are measured on the same answer key. The plainest one is the only one that can promise a result. This chapter covers hybrid search, reranking, contextual retrieval, metadata filtering and agentic search.7 min read✓ read
  5. 24When the Page Gives OrdersThe guard reads what strangers write, so it is the most exposed program in the building. The team watches a model obey a stranger. They learn the gap between a defence that lowers the odds and one that takes a power away. This chapter introduces prompt injection and the lethal trifecta.7 min read✓ read
  6. 25Grading a Thousand AnswersChecking by hand stops working at about fifty answers. This chapter covers three ways to mark an answer, how to test a model that grades other models, and error analysis. It is the most useful quality work in the field, and it needs no machine at all.7 min read✓ read
  7. 26What It Really Costs"It depends on tokens" is not an answer for a finance director. Anaya works out the true price of the guard. She finds three very different totals for the same tool. The cheapest fix is the order in which the guard's parts run. This chapter teaches the cascade.8 min read✓ read
5

The messy real world

Scans and photographs, what you may send, the rules, a spec for a thing that varies, and designing for the wrong answer.

  1. 27Paper, Photos and ScansUntil now, the guard only read text. Anaya checks fifty random attachments and finds that real traffic is mostly photographs. She also sees how a capital O in place of a zero can slip a number past a rule. This chapter teaches OCR and the document audit.7 min read✓ read
  2. 28What You May SendUntil now, the team has assumed the text could go to an outside company. Three questions, asked in a fixed order, tell you if it can. Then a vendor's terms of service say things nobody had read. This chapter teaches retention and data residency.8 min read✓ read
  3. 29Rules, Risk and ResponsibilityLakshmi tells what twenty years in a bank taught her about paperwork. Then the team writes a one-page document. It says what the guard is for, what it gets wrong and what it must never be used for. After that they try to delete one customer and find every place that customer's data lives. The chapter covers risk tiers, India's data protection law, system cards, deletion drills, human oversight and shadow AI.10 min read✓ read
  4. 30The Spec for a Thing That VariesA notice says a model will be retired in thirty days. It shows what a spec (the recipe card for a product) must hold when software does not act the same way twice. It also shows what the switch that turns the AI off should leave running. The chapter introduces rollback, the kill switch and pinned versions.8 min read✓ read
  5. 31Build, Buy or Teach ItA vendor offers to sell the team what it spent six months building. A founder suggests training a model of their own. Both ideas sound sensible, and each must pass the same test. The chapter introduces the AI value chain, open-weight models, fine-tuning and lock-in.9 min read✓ read
  6. 32Designing for the Wrong AnswerA tool that is right nine times in ten is wrong the tenth time. What the screen does then decides if people trust it. Next, a pilot built so it can fail gives a strange result. The tool works, and nothing changes. You meet refusals, pilots and failure thresholds.9 min read✓ read
6

Under the hood

The plumbing, choosing a model, retrieval that survives review, agents, voices and pictures, release gates, and assuming the worst.

  1. 33The Plumbing Under the MagicFor two hours the guard got something wrong, and no error showed anywhere. So Anaya learns to read the plain software around the one unpredictable part, like a plumber's diagram of pipes. You meet data contracts, Python, HTTP and status codes, environment variables, Git and experiment runners.8 min read✓ read
  2. 34Choosing a Model on Your Own CasesA founder wants to switch to whichever model topped last week's chart. The team does what you do before buying a car. They test-drive three models on their own roads, write the choice on a card, and plan what each model sees. You meet leaderboards, routing, model selection cards and provenance.8 min read✓ read
  3. 35Retrieval That Survives a ReviewA prototype works because you picked every document and you are the only user. Production takes both comforts away. In a review full of people who hope it fails, four questions are put to the chatbot. They fit every retrieval system. The chapter teaches ingestion, parsers, access control and abstention.9 min read✓ read
  4. 36Workflows, Agents and the Standard PlugA bank teller can look up a balance but cannot send money on a customer's word. Three questions about a support console are settled by crossing things out. How much should a model decide? How do you stop it? What does a standard plug promise, and what does it not? The chapter teaches tool contracts, idempotency, fixed workflows, bounded agents and MCP.11 min read✓ read
  5. 37Pages, Pictures and VoicesRead a railway timetable aloud, word by word, and nobody learns when the train leaves. The team finally takes on photographs and voice notes. They find the stage where meaning first goes wrong. They build a test that can tell a hearing mistake from a thinking one. The chapter teaches multimodal systems, speech-to-text, voice pipelines and speaker attribution.8 min read✓ read
  6. 38Gates, Traces and RollbacksA late Friday edit to one line of instructions, made with no test, shows why even a small change needs a gate. It also shows why a team should answer "why did it do that?" in forty seconds. You meet golden datasets, regressions, release gates, observability, trace records, p95 and canary releases.9 min read✓ read
  7. 39Assuming the WorstA compliance report, a Saturday spent trying to break the product for a prize of sweets, and a table that puts each safeguard next to its test. The model can be tricked, so the system around it has to be the defence. You meet attack surface, least privilege, red teaming, audit trails, risk registers and residual risk.9 min read✓ read
7

A real product, and a job

Shipping it, pricing it, growing it, counting it, running it with real users, and getting hired to do it.

  1. 40A Product, Not a DemoA dish cooked well for two people is not yet on the restaurant menu. Before the festival season, the team lists all that stands between a working prototype and a real service. For each big decision, they write what would make them reverse it. You meet the production delta, graceful degradation, staging, latency budgets, architecture decision records and exit cost.10 min read✓ read
  2. 41Shipping the Whole ThingIn December Anaya stands before the people who doubted her idea. Think of it as an oral exam at school. She tells them what she built, what broke, who used it, what it costs and what she does not know. The eleven stages she followed are the year she has just lived. You meet SDKs, findings documents, failure classes and evidence packs.10 min read✓ read
  3. 42Who Pays, and How MuchA lender's technical lead asks what the guard would cost him. The answer turns on three different people and four ways of charging. It also turns on one row of a table that most price lists never draw. You meet seat, usage, outcome and hybrid pricing, contribution margin, flywheels and gross margin.11 min read✓ read
  4. 43How People Find It and StayA tool that nobody finds protects nobody. Five developers get a README and nothing else, and a stopwatch shows where they give up. A spelling checker shows where the first moment of value must happen. You meet AARRR, activation, time-to-value, the Fogg behaviour model, product-led growth, growth loops, network effects, virality and dark patterns.9 min read✓ read
  5. 44Counting What MattersReal people now use the tool. So the question changes from "does it work?" to "what do they do?" A privacy tool must count without keeping what it hides. Then a small sum shows why a young company cannot run the test it wants. The chapter teaches the event taxonomy, the tracking plan, cohorts, A/B tests and the minimum detectable effect.9 min read✓ read
  6. 45The Tools and the HarnessA new engineer asks which tool is for what. A senior engineer answers with a drawing of empty slots, not a list of brands. Then the new engineer builds a weekly report twice, once with fixed steps and once with an agent, and the two are scored on the same twenty weeks. The chapter teaches toolchains, claim audits, the harness, project memory, allowlists, verifiers, sub-agents, state machines, feature flags, rollback triggers and incident reviews.13 min read✓ read
  7. 46Real People, Real UseA demo works while you watch it. A real product must work when nobody is watching, for people who owe you nothing. In spring, Anaya gets the guard ready for strangers. She finds honest early users and watches them without helping. Then she ships one change because of what she saw. You learn design partners, informed consent, observation sessions, changelogs and support logs.10 min read✓ read
  8. 47The Work, and the JobRhea used to run government technology programmes. She has built something real and does not know how to show it. Over a few Sunday evenings, Anaya helps her turn a year of work into a map of the jobs she wants, a page of proof, and rehearsed answers to the questions that decide the job. You learn role matrices, case studies, product sense, system-design interviews, the STAR method and take-homes.13 min read✓ read
